nodes.name: Theorem 1.1 (Bessel identity for the Waldspurger correspondence over $\BC$)
nodes.statement: Let $\pi $ be as above. There exists $\sigma$ as above such that for any $z \in \BC \smallsetminus \{0\}$ we have \begin{align} i_{\hskip 0.5 pt \pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} z / 4 & 1 \\ 1 & \end{pmatrix} = \frac {2 \epsilon (\pi, 1/2) \, \psi_1 \lp 2 / z \rp |z|} {L(\pi, 1/2)} j_{\sigma, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & - z\- \\ z \\ \end{pmatrix}, \end{align} in which $L (\pi, 1/2)$ and $\epsilon (\pi, 1/2)$ are the central values of the $L$-factor and the $\epsilon$-factor associated with $ \pi $.
nodes.statement_short: Every unitary $\pi$ of $\PGL_2(\BC)$ has a $\sigma$ on $\SL_2(\BC)$ whose Bessel function matches the relative Bessel function of $\pi$ up to $\epsilon/L$ factors.
assumptions: Let $\pi$ be an infinite-dimensional irreducible unitary representation of $\GL_2 (\BC)$ with trivial central character (that is, a representation of $ \PGL_2 (\BC)$).
Let $\sigma$ be an irreducible unitary representation of $\SL_2 (\BC)$.
conclusions: There exists $\sigma$ as above such that for any $z \in \BC \smallsetminus \{0\}$ we have \begin{align} i_{\hskip 0.5 pt \pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} z / 4 & 1 \\ 1 & \end{pmatrix} = \frac {2 \epsilon (\pi, 1/2) \, \psi_1 \lp 2 / z \rp |z|} {L(\pi, 1/2)} j_{\sigma, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & - z\- \\ z \\ \end{pmatrix}, \end{align}
in which $L (\pi, 1/2)$ and $\epsilon (\pi, 1/2)$ are the central values of the $L$-factor and the $\epsilon$-factor associated with $ \pi $.

nodes.name: Remark on the simplicity of the complex case
nodes.statement: Admittedly, the Waldspurger correspondence over $\BC$ is tremendously simpler than that over $\BR$, because all the double covers of $\SL_2 (\BC)$ are isomorphic to the trivial product $\SL_2 (\BC) \times \{\pm 1 \}$. Moreover, the representation theory of $\GL_2 (\BC)$ or $\SL_2 (\BC)$ is simpler as discrete series do not exist. Our expositions would be simplified if we view $\PGL_2 (\BC)$ as $\PSL_2 (\BC)$ and work only on $\SL_2 (\BC)$. Nevertheless, we choose to work in the framework of the representation theory of $\GL_2 (\BC)$ in order to preserve the analogy between this work and \cite{BaruchMao-Real}.

nodes.name: Remark on the use of the distributional variant of the integral formula
nodes.statement: It is the distributional variant of \eqref{eq: main 1} (see \eqref{6eq: Fourier}) that we shall use to deduce the formula of the relative Bessel function $i_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$. Critical is that the test function in \eqref{6eq: Fourier} only needs to be rapidly decaying at infinity but not zero. By using this variant, we may completely avoid the analysis of differential operators as in \cite{BaruchMao-Real}. This idea would also work in the real context as in \cite{BaruchMao-Real}.
nodes.statement_short: Using the distributional form of the Fourier formula avoids the differential-operator analysis of Baruch-Mao.

nodes.name: Basic notations $G$, $S$, $B$, $A$, $Z$, $N$, $\varw$, $\varw_0$, $s(a)$, $t(a)$, $z(c)$
nodes.statement: Let $G=\GL_2(\BC)$ and $S=\SL_2(\BC)$. Let $B $, $ A $ and $Z$ denote the Borel subgroup of upper triangular matrices, the diagonal subgroup and the center of $G$ respectively. Set \[ N=\left\{n(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&x \\ &1 \end{pmatrix}:x\in \BC \right\}, \] and \begin{align*} \varw = \begin{pmatrix} &-1 \\ 1& \end{pmatrix} &, \hskip 10 pt \varw_0=\begin{pmatrix} &1 \\ 1& \end{pmatrix}, \\ s(a) =\begin{pmatrix} a & \\ &a^{-1} \end{pmatrix} , \hskip 10 pt t(a)= &\begin{pmatrix} a& \\ &1 \end{pmatrix}, \hskip 10 pt z(c)=\begin{pmatrix} c& \\ &c \end{pmatrix}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Fixes $\GL_2(\BC)$, $\SL_2(\BC)$, their Borel, torus, centre, unipotent radical and the Weyl/torus matrices used throughout.

nodes.name: The additive character $\psi_{\lambdaup}$ and the self-dual measure on $\BC$
nodes.statement: Recall that $e (x) = e^{2 \pi i x}$. For $\lambdaup \in \BC$, let $\psi = \psi_{\lambdaup}$ be the additive character of $\BC$ defined by $$ \psi_{\lambdaup} (z)=e (\Tr \shskip (\lambdaup z)) = e (\lambdaup z + \overline {\lambdaup z}).$$ We also view $\psi$ as a character of $N$ by $\psi(n(z))=\psi(z)$. Let $\|z\| = |z|_{\BC}= |z|^2$. Take $dz = d_{\lambdaup} z$ to be $2 \sqrt { \|\lambdaup\|}$ times of the Lebesgue measure on $\BC$, which is self-dual with respect to $\psi$. Let $\BCx = \BC \smallsetminus \{0\}$. Set $\dx z=dz/\|z\| $.
nodes.statement_short: Defines $\psi_\lambdaup(z)=e(\Tr(\lambdaup z))$, the norm $\|z\|=|z|^2$, and the $\psi$-self-dual Haar measure.
differentia: defined by $$ \psi_{\lambdaup} (z)=e (\Tr \shskip (\lambdaup z)) = e (\lambdaup z + \overline {\lambdaup z}).$$

nodes.name: The $\psi$-Fourier transform
nodes.statement: For $f\in L^1(\BC )$, we define the $\psi$-Fourier transform of $f$ as \begin{equation} \widehat f(u)= \int_\BC f(z)\psi(uz)dz. \end{equation} With our choice of measure $d z$, the Fourier transform is self-dual, namely, $\widehat {\widehat f } (u) = f (-u)$.

nodes.name: The character $\chiup_{\nu, l}$ of $\BCx$
The principal series $\pi (\chiup_{\nu_1, l_1}, \chiup_{\nu_2, l_2})$ of $G$
nodes.statement_short: Irreducible admissible representations of $\GL_2(\BC)$ are the unique irreducible quotients of unitarily induced $\mathrm{Ind}_B^G$, parametrized by $(\nu_1,\nu_2,l_1,l_2)$.

nodes.name: The principal series $\pi_{\mu, m}$ of $G$
nodes.statement: For $\mu\in \BC, m\in \BZ$, we let $ \pi_{\mu,\shskip m}$ denote the principal series of $G$ with parameter $\big(\mu, - \mu, \frac 1 2 m, - \frac 1 2 m \big)$ if $m$ is even or $ \big(\mu, - \mu, \frac 1 2 (m+1), - \frac 1 2 (m-1) \big) $ if $m$ is odd. Note that $\pi_{\mu, \shskip m} \otimes \chiup_{\nu,\shskip l} (\det)$ exhaust all the principal series of $G$ as above. It is clear that $\pi_{\mu, \shskip m}$ has trivial central character if and only if $m$ is even.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_{\mu,m}$ is the principal series of $\GL_2(\BC)$ with parameter $(\mu,-\mu,\pm\frac12 m)$; trivial central character iff $m$ is even.

nodes.name: The principal series $\sigma_{\mu, m}$ of $S$
nodes.statement: When restricting $\pi_{\mu, \shskip m}$ on $S$, we obtain the principal series $\sigma_{\mu,\shskip m}$ of $S$ induced from the character $s(a) \ra \chiup_{ 2 \mu,\shskip m} (a) $. The principal series $\sigma_{\mu,\shskip m}$ exhaust all the irreducible admissible representations of $S$.
differentia: of $S$ induced from the character $s(a) \ra \chiup_{ 2 \mu,\shskip m} (a) $

nodes.name: Unitarity criterion for $\pi_{\mu, m}$ and $\sigma_{\mu, m}$
nodes.statement: Finally, the representation $\pi_{\mu, \shskip m}$ or $\sigma_{\mu, \shskip m}$ is unitary if \begin{itemize} \item[-] (unitary principal series) $\Re \mu = 0$, or \item[-] (complementary series) $\mu \in \lp 0, \frac 1 2\rp$ and $ m = 0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_{\mu,m}$ (resp. $\sigma_{\mu,m}$) is unitary exactly in the principal-series case $\Re\mu=0$ and the complementary-series case $\mu\in(0,\frac12)$, $m=0$.
nodes.origin_citation: Knapp, Representation Theory of Semisimple Groups
assumptions: Finally, the representation $\pi_{\mu, \shskip m}$ or $\sigma_{\mu, \shskip m}$
conclusions: (unitary principal series) $\Re \mu = 0$, or
(complementary series) $\mu \in \lp 0, \frac 1 2\rp$ and $ m = 0$.

nodes.name: Genericity: existence and uniqueness of the $\psi$-Whittaker functional
nodes.statement: It is well known that $\pi$ is generic in the sense that there exists a nonzero continuous $\psi$-Whittaker functional $L$ on $H_\infty$, unique up to scalars, satisfying \begin{equation*} L (\pi(n )\varv)=\psi(n )L(\varv), \hskip 10 pt n \in N, \ \varv\in H_\infty. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Every infinite-dimensional irreducible unitary $\pi$ of $G$ admits a $\psi$-Whittaker functional, unique up to scalars.
assumptions: Let $\pi$ be an infinite dimensional irreducible unitary representation of $G$ on a Hilbert space $H$, with $H_\infty$ its subspace of smooth vectors.
conclusions: there exists a nonzero continuous $\psi$-Whittaker functional $L$ on $H_\infty$, unique up to scalars, satisfying \begin{equation*} L (\pi(n )\varv)=\psi(n )L(\varv), \hskip 10 pt n \in N, \ \varv\in H_\infty. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: The Whittaker function $W_\varv(g)$
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} W_\varv(g)=L(\pi(g)\varv), \hskip 10 pt \varv\in H_\infty, \ g\in G, \end{equation} be the Whittaker function corresponding to $\varv$. All these definitions are valid for $S$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1 (asymptotics of $W_\varv(t(a))$ on the torus)
nodes.statement: For $\varv\in H_\infty$, the function $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ is rapidly decreasing at infinity and is of order $\|a\|^{\rho}$ for certain $\rho > 0$ when $a$ is in the vicinity of zero.
nodes.statement_short: Whittaker functions on the torus decay rapidly at infinity and vanish to a positive order $\|a\|^{\rho}$ at zero.
conclusions: the function $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ is rapidly decreasing at infinity and is of order $\|a\|^{\rho}$ for certain $\rho > 0$ when $a$ is in the vicinity of zero.

nodes.name: Jacquet-Shalika asymptotic expansion of Whittaker functions
nodes.statement: There is a finite set $C$ of characters of $\BCx$ with {\it positive} real part, namely, characters $\chiup $ with $|\chiup (z)| = \|z\|^{\rho}$ for $\rho > 0$, and for each $\chiup \in C$ a nonnegative integer $r_{\chiup}$ with the following property\footnote{For $\GL_2$, one should have $r_{\chiup} = 0$ or $1$.}: let $X$ be the set of finite functions of the form $\chiup (a) ( \log \|a\|)^{r}$, with $\chiup \in C$ and $r \leqslant r_{\chiup}$, then for any given $\varv \in H_{\infty}$ there are functions $\phi_{\xi}$ in the Schwartz space on $\BC \times \mathrm{U}_2(\BC)$ such that \begin{align*} W_{\varv} (t(a) k) = \sum_{ \xi\shskip \in X } \phi_{\xi} (a, k) \xi (a). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Whittaker functions expand as finite sums $\sum_\xi \phi_\xi(a,k)\xi(a)$ over finite functions $\xi$ built from positive-real-part characters.
assumptions: let $X$ be the set of finite functions of the form $\chiup (a) ( \log \|a\|)^{r}$, with $\chiup \in C$ and $r \leqslant r_{\chiup}$
conclusions: W_{\varv} (t(a) k) = \sum_{ \xi\shskip \in X } \phi_{\xi} (a, k) \xi (a).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: The rapid decay of $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ as $\|a\| \ra \infty$ is already proven in \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement} (and also \cite[\S 6]{J-L}), in particular (68)-(72). However, we do not find any concrete statement in either \cite{J-L} or \cite{Godement} on the asymptotic of $W_{\varv} (t(a) )$ for $a$ small. Nevertheless, we may prove the asymptotic $W_{\varv} (t(a)) = O (\|a\|^{\rho}) $ as $\|a\| \ra 0$ if we examine and estimate the integrals in (69) and (70) in \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement} more carefully; it is important here that $\pi$ is unitary so that either $\Re \mu = 0$ or $\mu \in \lp 0, \frac 1 2 \rp$ (we may choose $0 < \rho < \frac 1 2 - \Re \mu$). It should be noted that only $\mathrm{U}_2 (\BC)$-finite vectors are treated in \cite[\S 6]{J-L} and \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement}.
nodes.statement_short: Cite Godement for rapid decay at infinity, then re-estimate his integrals (69)-(70) to get the $\|a\|^{\rho}$ bound near zero, using unitarity of $\pi$.

nodes.name: Rapid decay at infinity is known
nodes.statement: The rapid decay of $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ as $\|a\| \ra \infty$ is already proven in \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement} (and also \cite[\S 6]{J-L}), in particular (68)-(72).
nodes.statement_short: Quote Godement and Jacquet-Langlands for the decay of $W_\varv(t(a))$ as $\|a\|\ra\infty$.

nodes.statement: However, we do not find any concrete statement in either \cite{J-L} or \cite{Godement} on the asymptotic of $W_{\varv} (t(a) )$ for $a$ small.
nodes.statement_short: Note the gap: the literature has no explicit small-$a$ asymptotic.

nodes.name: Re-estimate Godement's integrals near zero
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, we may prove the asymptotic $W_{\varv} (t(a)) = O (\|a\|^{\rho}) $ as $\|a\| \ra 0$ if we examine and estimate the integrals in (69) and (70) in \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement} more carefully; it is important here that $\pi$ is unitary so that either $\Re \mu = 0$ or $\mu \in \lp 0, \frac 1 2 \rp$ (we may choose $0 < \rho < \frac 1 2 - \Re \mu$).

nodes.name: Lemma 2.2 (Fourier-uniqueness for $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))$)
nodes.statement: Let $\varv\in H_\infty$, $f,g\in C^\infty(\BCx)$. Assume that both $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ and $g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ are in $L^1(\BCx, \dx a)$. If \[ \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{\pi(n)\varv}(t(a))\dx a=\int_{\BCx} g(a)W_{\pi(n)\varv}(t(a))\dx a \] for all $n\in N$, then $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))=g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ for all $a\in \BCx$.
nodes.statement_short: If two integrals against $W_{\pi(n)\varv}(t(a))$ agree for all $n\in N$, then $fW_\varv = gW_\varv$ pointwise.
assumptions: Assume that both $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ and $g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ are in $L^1(\BCx, \dx a)$.
If \[ \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{\pi(n)\varv}(t(a))\dx a=\int_{\BCx} g(a)W_{\pi(n)\varv}(t(a))\dx a \] for all $n\in N$,
conclusions: then $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))=g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ for all $a\in \BCx$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: The proof is literally the same as that of \cite[Lemma 2.1]{BaruchMao-Real}. We have \begin{align*} \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{\pi(n(x))\varv}(t(a))\dx a = \hskip -1 pt \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) n(x))\dx a = \hskip -1 pt \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) \psi (ax) \dx a. \end{align*} Hence follows the integrability of the first integral for all $x \in \BC$ and it is equal to the Fourier transform of the function $\|a\|\- f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $. The identity in the lemma then yields the equality between the Fourier transform of $\|a\|\- f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $ and that of $\|a\|\- g (a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $. It follows that $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))=g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ for all $a\in \BCx$.
nodes.statement_short: Recognize both sides as Fourier transforms of $\|a\|^{-1}fW_\varv$ and $\|a\|^{-1}gW_\varv$ and invert.

nodes.name: Translate the Whittaker function by $n(x)$
nodes.statement: The proof is literally the same as that of \cite[Lemma 2.1]{BaruchMao-Real}. We have \begin{align*} \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{\pi(n(x))\varv}(t(a))\dx a = \hskip -1 pt \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) n(x))\dx a = \hskip -1 pt \int_{\BCx} f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) \psi (ax) \dx a. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use $(\psi,N)$-equivariance to rewrite $W_{\pi(n(x))\varv}(t(a))$ as $W_\varv(t(a))\psi(ax)$.

nodes.name: Identify the integral as a Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Hence follows the integrability of the first integral for all $x \in \BC$ and it is equal to the Fourier transform of the function $\|a\|\- f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $.
nodes.statement_short: Recognize the integral as the Fourier transform of $\|a\|^{-1}f(a)W_\varv(t(a))$.

nodes.name: Invert the Fourier transform
nodes.statement: The identity in the lemma then yields the equality between the Fourier transform of $\|a\|\- f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $ and that of $\|a\|\- g (a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $. It follows that $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))=g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ for all $a\in \BCx$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality of Fourier transforms forces equality of the functions.

nodes.name: Normalization of the Whittaker functional by the inner product
nodes.statement: Let $\langle \, ,\shskip \rangle $ be a $G$-invariant nonzero inner product on $H$. We can normalize the Whittaker functional $L$ so that \begin{equation} \langle \varv_1,\varv_2\rangle =\int_{\BCx}W_{\varv_1}(t(a))\overline {W_{\varv_2}(t(a))}\dx a. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalize $L$ so that the $G$-invariant inner product is the torus integral of $W_{\varv_1}\overline{W_{\varv_2}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$

nodes.name: The normalized torus invariant functional $P$
nodes.statement: We define \begin{equation} P(\varv)=\frac{1}{L(\pi,1/2)}\int_{\BCx} W_\varv(t(a))\dx a, \hskip 10 pt \varv \in H_{\infty}, \end{equation} in which the normalization factor $L(\pi, 1/2)$ is the central value of the $L$-function for $\pi$ (see for example \cite[\S 4]{Knapp}).
nodes.statement_short: $P(\varv)$ is the torus integral of $W_\varv$ divided by the central $L$-value $L(\pi,1/2)$.
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$

nodes.name: $P$ is the unique $A$-invariant continuous functional
nodes.statement: In view of Lemma \ref{lem: asymptotic of W(t(a))}, the integral above is absolutely convergent. Moreover, it may be verified that $P$ is a nonzero continuous linear functional on $H_\infty$ satisfying \[ P(\pi(a)\varv)= P(\varv), \hskip 10 pt a \in A, \ \varv\in H_\infty, \] if the central character of $\pi $ is trivial. Hence $P$ is the nonzero unique up to scalar continuous linear functional with the above invariance property.
nodes.statement_short: $P$ converges absolutely and is, up to scalars, the unique continuous $A$-invariant functional on $H_\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$
assumptions: if the central character of $\pi $ is trivial.
conclusions: $P$ is a nonzero continuous linear functional on $H_\infty$ satisfying \[ P(\pi(a)\varv)= P(\varv), \hskip 10 pt a \in A, \ \varv\in H_\infty, \]
Hence $P$ is the nonzero unique up to scalar continuous linear functional with the above invariance property.

nodes.name: The vector $\varv_{\lambda, f}$ attached to a functional and a test function
nodes.statement: For every continuous linear functional $\lambda $ on $H_\infty$ and every $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, the map $\varv\to \lambda(\pi(f)\varv)$ is continuous on $H$ by \cite[Proposition 3.2]{Shalika-MO}. By the Riesz representation theorem, there exists a unique vector $\varv_{\lambda,\shskip f}$ such that \begin{equation} \lambda (\pi(f)\varv)=\langle \varv,\varv_{\lambda,\shskip f}\rangle , \hskip 10 pt \text{ all } \varv\in H_\infty. \end{equation} More concretely, for any orthonormal basis $\{ \varv_{\mathfrak i} \}$ in $H_{\infty}$, \begin{align} \varv_{\lambda,\shskip f} = \sum \overline {\lambda (\pi(f)\varv_{\mathfrak i})} \shskip \varv_{\mathfrak i} . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Riesz representation gives a unique $\varv_{\lambda,f}$ with $\lambda(\pi(f)\varv)=\langle\varv,\varv_{\lambda,f}\rangle$.
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$

nodes.name: The Bessel distribution $J_{\pi,\psi}$ and the relative Bessel distribution $I_{\pi,\psi}$
nodes.statement: Then we define the Bessel distribution by \begin{equation} J(f)=J_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(f)=\overline{L(\varv_{L, \shskip f})} \end{equation} and the relative Bessel distribution by \begin{equation} I(f)=I_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(f)=\overline{L(\varv_{P, \shskip f}) }. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $J(f)=\overline{L(\varv_{L,f})}$ and $I(f)=\overline{L(\varv_{P,f})}$.
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$

nodes.name: Orthonormal-basis expansions of $J(f)$ and $I(f)$
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{3eq: orthonormal basis}, for any orthonormal basis $\{ \varv_{\mathfrak i} \}$ in $H_{\infty}$, we have \begin{align} J (f) = \sum L (\pi(f)\varv_{\mathfrak i}) \overline {L (\varv_{\mathfrak i})}, \end{align} and \begin{align} I (f) = \sum P (\pi(f)\varv_{\mathfrak i}) \overline {L (\varv_{\mathfrak i})}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Both distributions are sums over an orthonormal basis of $L$ or $P$ applied to $\pi(f)\varv_{\mathfrak i}$.
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$

nodes.name: $I(f)$ as a torus integral of left translates of $J$
nodes.statement: Letting $\widetilde f(g)=f(g^{-1})$, it follows from \cite[Corollary 23.7]{BaruchMao-Real} that $J(f)=L(\varv_{L,\shskip\widetilde f})$ and $I(f)=P(\varv_{L,\shskip\widetilde f})$. Thus \[ I(f)=P(\varv_{L,\shskip\widetilde f})=\frac{1}{L(\pi,1/2)}\int_{\BCx} W_{\varv_{L,\shskip \widetilde f}}(t(a))\dx a=\frac{1}{L(\pi,1/2)}\int_{\BCx} L(\pi(t(a))\varv_{L,\shskip \widetilde f})\dx a. \] Let $\rho_l$ denote the left translation of functions on $G$, namely, $(\rho_l (h) f)(g) = f (h\- g)$. Note that for any $\varv\in H_\infty$ \begin{align*} \pi((\rho_l(t(a))f)^{\sim}) \varv & = \int_G f(t(a\-) g\-)\pi(g) \varv \shskip dg \\ & =\int_G f(g\-)\pi(g)\pi(t(a\-)) \varv\shskip dg = \pi (\widetilde f) \pi (t(a\-)) \varv, \end{align*} and therefore $\pi(t(a))\varv_{L,\shskip\widetilde f}=\varv_{L,\shskip (\rho_l(t(a))f)^{\sim}}$. Hence \begin{equation} I(f)=\frac{1}{L(\pi,1/2)}\int_{\BCx}J(\rho_l(t(a))f)\dx a. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The relative Bessel distribution is the torus average of $J$ over left translations $\rho_l(t(a))$, divided by $L(\pi,1/2)$.
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$

nodes.name: The Bessel distribution $J_{\sigma, \psi}$ for $S$
nodes.statement: Finally, we define Bessel distributions for $S$ in the same manner. Let $(\sigma, H)$ be a unitary representation of $S$. Let $L$ be a nonzero continuous $\psi$-Whittaker functional on $H_\infty$. Similar as above, for any $h\in C_c^\infty(S)$, there exists a unique vector $\varv_{L,\shskip h} \in H$ such that \begin{equation} L (\varv_{L,\shskip h})=\langle \varv,\varv_{L,\shskip h} \rangle, \hskip 10 pt \text{ all } \varv \in H_\infty. \end{equation} Then one can define similarly the Bessel distribution $J_{\sigma,\shskip \psi}$ on $S$ associated with $\sigma$ by \begin{equation} J_{\sigma,\shskip \psi}(h)=\overline {L (\varv_{L,\shskip h})}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Bessel and relative Bessel distributions for $\GL_2 (\BC)$

nodes.name: The function $J_{\mu, m}(z)$
nodes.statement: Let $\mu \in \BC $ and $m \in \BZ $. We define \begin{equation} J_{\mu,\shskip m} (z) = J_{- 2\mu - \frac 12 m } \lp z \rp J_{- 2\mu + \frac 12 m } \lp {\overline z} \rp. \end{equation} The function $J_{\mu,\shskip m} (z)$ is well defined in the sense that the expression on the right of \eqref{0def: J mu m (z)} is independent on the choice of the argument of $z$ modulo $2 \pi$.
nodes.statement_short: Product $J_{-2\mu-\frac12 m}(z)J_{-2\mu+\frac12 m}(\overline z)$ of classical Bessel functions, independent of the branch of $\arg z$.
nodes.origin_citation: Qi, Theory of Fundamental Bessel Functions of High Rank (arXiv:1612.03553)

nodes.name: The Bessel function $\bfJ_{\mu, m}(z)$ over the complex numbers
nodes.statement: Next, we define \begin{equation} \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp = \left\{ \begin{split} & \frac {2 \pi^2} {\sin (2\pi \mu)} \lp J_{\mu,\shskip m} (4 \pi \sqrt z) - J_{-\mu,\shskip -m} (4 \pi \sqrt z) \rp, \hskip 6.5 pt \text {if } m \text{ is even},\\ & \frac {2 \pi^2 i} {\cos (2\pi \mu)} \lp J_{\mu,\shskip m} (4 \pi \sqrt z) + J_{-\mu,\shskip -m} (4 \pi \sqrt z) \rp, \hskip 5 pt \text {if } m \text{ is odd}, \end{split} \right. \end{equation} where $\sqrt z$ is the principal branch of the square root, and it is understood that in the nongeneric case when $4 \mu \in 2\BZ + m$ the right hand side should be replaced by its limit. $\bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp$ is a well defined function on $\BCx$ only when $m$ is even, but it becomes well defined after multiplying the factor $\sqrt { z / |z|} $ when $m$ is odd.
nodes.statement_short: A normalized combination of $J_{\pm\mu,\pm m}(4\pi\sqrt z)$, well defined on $\BCx$ for even $m$ (and after a $\sqrt{z/|z|}$ twist for odd $m$).
nodes.origin_citation: Qi, Theory of Fundamental Bessel Functions of High Rank (arXiv:1612.03553)

nodes.name: Lemma 4.1 (crude bounds for $\bfJ_{\mu, m}$)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $|\Re \mu | < \rho$. We have \begin{equation*} \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp \lll \left\{\begin{split} & 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho}, \hskip 11 pt \text{ if } |z| \leqslant 1, \\ & 1 /{\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}, \hskip 10 pt \text{ if } |z| > 1, \end{split}\right. \end{equation*} with the implied constant depending only on $\mu$, $\rho$ and $m$. In particular, \begin{equation*} \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp \lll 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho} + 1 / {\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}. \end{equation*}
conclusions: \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp \lll \left\{\begin{split} & 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho}, \hskip 11 pt \text{ if } |z| \leqslant 1, \\ & 1 /{\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}, \hskip 10 pt \text{ if } |z| > 1, \end{split}\right. \end{equation*} with the implied constant depending only on $\mu$, $\rho$ and $m$.
In particular, \begin{equation*} \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp \lll 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho} + 1 / {\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}.

nodes.name: The Bessel function $j_{\pi, \psi}$ for $\GL_2 (\BC)$
nodes.statement: As defined in \S \ref{sec: notations}, let $\pi = \pi_{\mu, \shskip m}$ be a principal series representation of $G = \GL_2 (\BC)$, and, for $\lambdaup \in \BCx$, let $\psi = \psi_{\lambdaup} $ be a nontrivial additive character on $N$. The central character $\omega_{\pi} (z (c)) = c /|c|$ if $m$ is odd and $ \omega_{\pi} (z (c)) \equiv 1$ if $m$ is even. We define a function $j = j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ supported on the open Bruhat cell $X = B \varw_0 B$ such that \begin{equation} j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ) = \left\{ \begin{split} & |\lambdaup a| \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp - \lambdaup^2 a \rp, \hskip 42 pt \text {if } m \text{ is even},\\ & - i |\lambdaup| {\textstyle \sqrt { |a| a}} \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp - \lambdaup^2 a \rp, \hskip 5 pt \text {if } m \text{ is odd}, \end{split} \right. \end{equation} \footnote{In \cite{Qi-Bessel}, as well as \cite{CPS}, the measure is not normalized by the factor $\sqrt {\|\lambdaup\|}$ and the choice of Weyl element is $\varw$ instead of $\varw_0$, so the Bessel functions in \cite[Proposition 18.5]{Qi-Bessel} are slightly different.} and that $j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ is left and right $ (\psi, N)$-equivariant and also $(\omega_{\pi}, Z)$-equivariant, namely, \begin{align} j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} \lp n(x)z(c) t(a) \varw_0 n(y) \rp = \psi (x) \psi (y) \omega_{\pi} (c ) j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $j_{\pi,\psi}$ is supported on the open Bruhat cell, equals $|\lambdaup a|\bfJ_{\mu,m}(-\lambdaup^2 a)$ on $t(a)\varw_0$, and is $(\psi,N)$- and $(\omega_\pi,Z)$-equivariant.
differentia: supported on the open Bruhat cell $X = B \varw_0 B$
is left and right $ (\psi, N)$-equivariant and also $(\omega_{\pi}, Z)$-equivariant

nodes.name: Kernel formula for the action of the Weyl element
nodes.statement: According to \cite[\S 18]{Qi-Bessel}, we have \begin{equation} W_{\varv} \lp t (b) \varw_0 \rp = \int_{\BCx } \omega_\pi ( a )\- j ( t(ab) \varw_0) W_{\varv} \lp t (a) \rp \dx a, \hskip 10 pt \text{ all } \varv \in H_{\infty}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Weyl-element action on the Whittaker model is a Hankel transform with kernel the Bessel function $j$.
conclusions: W_{\varv} \lp t (b) \varw_0 \rp = \int_{\BCx } \omega_\pi ( a )\- j ( t(ab) \varw_0) W_{\varv} \lp t (a) \rp \dx a,

nodes.name: Theorem 4.2 (Whittaker function on the open Bruhat cell)
nodes.statement: Let $\varv \in H_{\infty}$. Then \begin{align} W_{\varv} \lp g \rp = \int_{\BCx } j \big( g t \big( a\- \big) \big) W_{\varv} \lp t (a) \rp \dx a, \end{align} for all $ g \in B \varw_0 B$.
nodes.statement_short: On $B\varw_0 B$, $W_\varv(g)$ is the integral of $j(gt(a^{-1}))W_\varv(t(a))$ over $\BCx$.
conclusions: W_{\varv} \lp g \rp = \int_{\BCx } j \big( g t \big( a\- \big) \big) W_{\varv} \lp t (a) \rp \dx a,

nodes.name: Restriction of $j_{\pi, \psi}$ to $\SL_2 (\BC)$
nodes.statement: It readily follows from (\ref{4eq : j = J}, \ref{4eq: psi variant}) that the restriction of the Bessel function $j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ on $S = \SL_2 (\BC)$ is given by \begin{align} j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} ( s (a) \varw ) = (-1)^m \left|\lambdaup a^2 \right| \bfJ_{ \mu,\shskip m} \lp \lambdaup^2 a^2 \rp, \end{align} and \begin{align} j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} \lp n(x) s (a) \varw n(y) \rp = \psi (x) \psi (y) j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} ( s (a) \varw ). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: On $s(a)\varw$ the Bessel function equals $(-1)^m|\lambdaup a^2|\bfJ_{\mu,m}(\lambdaup^2 a^2)$ and is two-sided $(\psi,N)$-equivariant.

nodes.name: Remark 4.3 (simpler kernel formula on $\SL_2 (\BC)$)
nodes.statement: Of course, the factor $ \omega_\pi ( a )\-$ in \eqref{4eq: Weyl element action} disappears if $\pi $ is a representation of $\PGL_2 (\BC)$ in the case when $m$ is even. Otherwise, it will be gone if one uses $s (a)$ instead of $t (a)$ for torus elements, so the kernel formula looks simpler for $\SL_2 (\BC)$, \begin{equation} W_{\varv} \lp s (b) \varw \rp = \int_{\BCx } j ( s(ab) \varw ) W_{\varv} \lp s (a) \rp \dx a, \end{equation} for all $\varv \in H_{\infty}$. See \cite[Theorem 2]{Mo-Kernel} and \cite[Theorem 2.3]{Baruch-Kernel}.
nodes.statement_short: The central-character factor disappears for $\PGL_2(\BC)$, or if $s(a)$ replaces $t(a)$.

nodes.name: Extension of $j$ to $G$ by zero
nodes.statement: We extend the definition of $j $ to the whole group $G$ by setting $j (g)=0$ for $g\notin X $.

nodes.name: Proposition 4.4 (local integrability of the Bessel function $j$)
nodes.statement: Assume that $\pi $ is unitary. Then $j $ is locally integrable over $G$. Namely, for any $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, we have \[ \int_G \left|f(g)j (g) \right| dg<\infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: For unitary $\pi$ the Bessel function $j$ is locally integrable on $G$.
conclusions: Then $j $ is locally integrable over $G$.
for any $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, we have \[ \int_G \left|f(g)j (g) \right| dg<\infty. \]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.4
nodes.statement: Recall that the measure on $X = NA \varw_0 N$ is given by $ d g = |a|^{-2} d x \hskip 1 pt \dx a \hskip 1 pt \dx c \hskip 1 pt d y$ if $g = n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y)$. We have \begin{align*} \int_G |f(g)j (g)| dg = \ & \int_{X}|f(g)j (g)|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(a)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y))|dxdy\dx c \right) |a|^{-2}\dx a \\ = \ & \int |j (t(a)\varw_0)| \lp \int J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) \dx c \rp |a|^{-2} \dx a, \end{align*} where $ J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}. In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is zero for small $|a|$ and of the order $|a|^{1+\varepsilon}$ for large $|a|$. In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $ {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$ when $|a|$ is large. It is now clear that the integral above is convergent.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $dg$ on the Bruhat cell, bound the inner orbital integral by Proposition A.1 and $j$ by Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: Decompose the integral over the Bruhat cell
nodes.statement: Recall that the measure on $X = NA \varw_0 N$ is given by $ d g = |a|^{-2} d x \hskip 1 pt \dx a \hskip 1 pt \dx c \hskip 1 pt d y$ if $g = n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y)$. We have \begin{align*} \int_G |f(g)j (g)| dg = \ & \int_{X}|f(g)j (g)|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(a)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y))|dxdy\dx c \right) |a|^{-2}\dx a \\ = \ & \int |j (t(a)\varw_0)| \lp \int J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) \dx c \rp |a|^{-2} \dx a, \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $dg$ in Bruhat coordinates and factor the integral through the orbital integral $J(\sqrt a, c, |f|)$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition A.1 to the inner integral
nodes.statement: where $ J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}. In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is zero for small $|a|$ and of the order $|a|^{1+\varepsilon}$ for large $|a|$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition A.1 makes the $c$-integral vanish for small $|a|$ and $O(|a|^{1+\varepsilon})$ for large $|a|$.

nodes.name: Bound $j(t(a)\varw_0)$ by Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $ {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$ when $|a|$ is large.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 bounds $j(t(a)\varw_0)$ by $|a|^{1/2}$ for large $|a|$.

nodes.name: Conclude convergence
nodes.statement: It is now clear that the integral above is convergent.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.1 (torus integral of right translates of $J$)
nodes.statement: Let $\varv\in H_\infty$, then \[ \int_{\BCx}J(\rho_r(t(a))f)W_{\varv}(t(a))\dx a=\int_Gf(g)W_{\varv}(g)dg, \] in which $\rho_r$ is the right translation, that is, $(\rho_r (h) f)(g) = f ( g h)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\int_{\BCx}J(\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))\dx a$ equals $\int_G f(g)W_\varv(g)dg$.
assumptions: in which $\rho_r$ is the right translation, that is, $(\rho_r (h) f)(g) = f ( g h)$.
conclusions: \int_{\BCx}J(\rho_r(t(a))f)W_{\varv}(t(a))\dx a=\int_Gf(g)W_{\varv}(g)dg,

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \cite[Lemma 7.1]{BaruchMao-Real}. For any $\varv\in H_\infty$, we have \begin{align*} \pi(\rho_r(t(a))f) \varv & = \int_G f(gt(a))\pi(g) \varv \shskip dg \\ & =\int_G f(g)\pi(g)\pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv\shskip dg = \pi (f) \pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv. \end{align*} Thus it follow from \eqref{def: vector v l f}, \eqref{def: J (f)} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)} that $\varv_{L,\hskip 1 pt \rho_r(t(a))f}=\pi(t(a))\varv_{L, \shskip f}$ and $J (\rho_r(t(a))f)=\overline {W_{\varv_{L, \shskip f}}(t(a))}$. Hence, in view of \eqref{eq: inner product}, we have \[ \int_{\BCx} J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))\dx a=\langle \varv,\varv_{L, \shskip f} \rangle. \] On the other hand, by \eqref{def: vector v l f} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)}, \[ \langle \varv,\varv_{L, \shskip f} \rangle =L(\pi(f)\varv)=\int_G f(g)W_\varv(g)dg, \] which finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\varv_{L,\rho_r(t(a))f}=\pi(t(a))\varv_{L,f}$, so the integral is $\langle\varv,\varv_{L,f}\rangle=L(\pi(f)\varv)$.

nodes.name: Right translation of $f$ moves onto $\pi(t(a^{-1}))$
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \cite[Lemma 7.1]{BaruchMao-Real}. For any $\varv\in H_\infty$, we have \begin{align*} \pi(\rho_r(t(a))f) \varv & = \int_G f(gt(a))\pi(g) \varv \shskip dg \\ & =\int_G f(g)\pi(g)\pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv\shskip dg = \pi (f) \pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Change variables to get $\pi(\rho_r(t(a))f)\varv = \pi(f)\pi(t(a^{-1}))\varv$.

nodes.name: Identify $\varv_{L,\rho_r(t(a))f}$ and $J(\rho_r(t(a))f)$
nodes.statement: Thus it follow from \eqref{def: vector v l f}, \eqref{def: J (f)} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)} that $\varv_{L,\hskip 1 pt \rho_r(t(a))f}=\pi(t(a))\varv_{L, \shskip f}$ and $J (\rho_r(t(a))f)=\overline {W_{\varv_{L, \shskip f}}(t(a))}$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce $\varv_{L,\rho_r(t(a))f}=\pi(t(a))\varv_{L,f}$ and $J(\rho_r(t(a))f)=\overline{W_{\varv_{L,f}}(t(a))}$.

nodes.name: Evaluate the torus integral as an inner product
nodes.statement: Hence, in view of \eqref{eq: inner product}, we have \[ \int_{\BCx} J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))\dx a=\langle \varv,\varv_{L, \shskip f} \rangle. \]
nodes.statement_short: The normalized inner product turns the integral into $\langle\varv,\varv_{L,f}\rangle$.

nodes.name: Compute the same inner product as $\int_G f W_\varv$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by \eqref{def: vector v l f} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)}, \[ \langle \varv,\varv_{L, \shskip f} \rangle =L(\pi(f)\varv)=\int_G f(g)W_\varv(g)dg, \] which finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: On the other hand $\langle\varv,\varv_{L,f}\rangle=L(\pi(f)\varv)=\int_G f(g)W_\varv(g)dg$.

nodes.name: The distribution $\widetilde J_{\pi, \psi}$ represented by $j$
nodes.statement: Recall the definition of the Bessel function $ j = j_{\pi,\shskip \psi} $ in the last section. We define a distribution $\widetilde J = \widetilde J_{\pi,\shskip \psi}$ on $C_c^\infty(G)$ by \[ \widetilde J (f)=\int_{G}f(g)j(g)dg. \] This distribution is well defined as we have proven in Proposition \ref{thm: local integrability} that $j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(g)$ is locally integrable on $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $\widetilde J(f)=\int_G f(g)j(g)dg$, well defined by Proposition 4.4.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.2 (torus integral of right translates of $\widetilde J$)
nodes.statement: \footnote{Lemma \ref{le42} is stronger than Lemma 7.2 in \cite{BaruchMao-Real} as our computation shows that it is not necessary to assume that $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ has a high order of vanishing at $a = 0$.} Let $\varv\in H_\infty$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$. Then \[ \int_{\BCx} \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a)) f)W_{\varv}(t(a))\dx a=\int_G f(g)W_{\varv}(g)dg. \]
nodes.statement_short: The same identity as Lemma 5.1 holds with $\widetilde J$ in place of $J$, with no vanishing hypothesis on $W_\varv$ at $0$.
conclusions: \int_{\BCx} \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a)) f)W_{\varv}(t(a))\dx a=\int_G f(g)W_{\varv}(g)dg.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} & \hskip 13 pt \int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a)) f)W_{\varv}(t(a))\dx a \\ &= \int \left(\int_{X}f(gt(a))j (g)dg\right) W_\varv(t(a)) \dx a \\ &= \int \left( \int_{X}f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))dg \right) W_\varv(t(a))\dx a \\ &= \int_{X} f(g) \left( \int j (gt(a^{-1}))W_\varv(t(a))\dx a \right)dg \\ &= \int_{X} f(g)W_\varv(g)dg. \end{align*} Here we have obtained the last equality from \eqref{thm: W(g) on BwB} in Theorem \ref{thm: W(g) on BwB}. It is however needed to justify the change of order of integrations in the second to the last equality. For this, it suffices to verify the absolute convergence of the integral in the third line. Note that \begin{align*} &\int_{X}|f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(b)\varw_0n(y))|dxdy\dx c \right) |b|^{-2}\dx b \\ = \ & \int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)| \lp \int J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) \dx c \rp |b|^{-2} \dx b, \end{align*} where $ J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}. In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is dominated by $ |b|^{1 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b)$ for some constant $B$, with $\Upsilon_B$ the characteristic function on $\{ b: |b| \geqslant B \}$. Since $\pi = \pi_{\mu, \shskip m}$ is unitary, we have $|\Re \mu | < \frac 1 2$. In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $1 + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. Consequently, we have the following estimations for the integral above \begin{align*} \lll \int \big( 1 + {|ab|}^{\frac 1 2} \big) |b|^{- 3 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b) d b \lll 1 + |a|^{\frac 1 2}. \end{align*} Finally, recall from Lemma \ref{lem: asymptotic of W(t(a))} that $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ is rapidly decreasing at infinity and of the order $|a|^{2\rho}$ near zero for certain $\rho > 0$, then follows the absolute convergence of the integral.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold $\widetilde J$, exchange the order of integration (justified by Proposition A.1, Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 2.1) and apply Theorem 4.2.

nodes.name: Unfold and apply Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} & \hskip 13 pt \int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a)) f)W_{\varv}(t(a))\dx a \\ &= \int \left(\int_{X}f(gt(a))j (g)dg\right) W_\varv(t(a)) \dx a \\ &= \int \left( \int_{X}f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))dg \right) W_\varv(t(a))\dx a \\ &= \int_{X} f(g) \left( \int j (gt(a^{-1}))W_\varv(t(a))\dx a \right)dg \\ &= \int_{X} f(g)W_\varv(g)dg. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Chain of equalities ending in $\int_X f(g)W_\varv(g)dg$ via Theorem 4.2.

nodes.name: Reduce to absolute convergence
nodes.statement: Here we have obtained the last equality from \eqref{thm: W(g) on BwB} in Theorem \ref{thm: W(g) on BwB}. It is however needed to justify the change of order of integrations in the second to the last equality. For this, it suffices to verify the absolute convergence of the integral in the third line.
nodes.statement_short: Justifying the interchange reduces to absolute convergence of the third-line integral.

nodes.name: Bound the inner orbital integral by Proposition A.1
nodes.statement: Note that \begin{align*} &\int_{X}|f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(b)\varw_0n(y))|dxdy\dx c \right) |b|^{-2}\dx b \\ = \ & \int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)| \lp \int J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) \dx c \rp |b|^{-2} \dx b, \end{align*} where $ J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}. In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is dominated by $ |b|^{1 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b)$ for some constant $B$, with $\Upsilon_B$ the characteristic function on $\{ b: |b| \geqslant B \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition A.1 dominates the $c$-integral by $|b|^{1+\varepsilon}\Upsilon_B(b)$.

nodes.name: Bound $j$ by Lemma 4.1 and estimate
nodes.statement: Since $\pi = \pi_{\mu, \shskip m}$ is unitary, we have $|\Re \mu | < \frac 1 2$. In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $1 + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. Consequently, we have the following estimations for the integral above \begin{align*} \lll \int \big( 1 + {|ab|}^{\frac 1 2} \big) |b|^{- 3 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b) d b \lll 1 + |a|^{\frac 1 2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Unitarity gives $|\Re\mu|<\frac12$, so Lemma 4.1 bounds $j$ by $1+|a|^{1/2}$ and the integral by $1+|a|^{1/2}$.

nodes.name: Conclude with the Whittaker asymptotics
nodes.statement: Finally, recall from Lemma \ref{lem: asymptotic of W(t(a))} that $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ is rapidly decreasing at infinity and of the order $|a|^{2\rho}$ near zero for certain $\rho > 0$, then follows the absolute convergence of the integral.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.1's decay of $W_\varv(t(a))$ gives absolute convergence.

nodes.name: Corollary 5.3 ($J$ is represented by the Bessel function $j$)
nodes.statement: The two distributions $\widetilde J $ and $J $ are the same. That is, for any $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, we have \[ J (f)=\int_G f(g)j (g)dg. \]
nodes.statement_short: $J(f)=\int_G f(g)j(g)dg$ for all test functions, i.e. $\widetilde J = J$.
conclusions: The two distributions $\widetilde J $ and $J $ are the same.
J (f)=\int_G f(g)j (g)dg.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.3
nodes.statement: Choose $\varv\in H_\infty$ with $W_{\varv} (1) = 1$, say. By Lemma \ref{le41} and \ref{le42} we have \[ \int J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))\dx a=\int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))\dx a \] for all $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$. We replace $\varv$ by $\pi(n)\varv$ for any $n\in N$ and apply Lemma \ref{le21}, it follows that \[ J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))=\widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a)) \] for all $a\in \BCx$. Letting $a = 1$, the conclusion follows immediately.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 make the two torus integrals agree; Lemma 2.2 then forces $J=\widetilde J$, and $a=1$ finishes.

nodes.name: Combine Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2
nodes.statement: Choose $\varv\in H_\infty$ with $W_{\varv} (1) = 1$, say. By Lemma \ref{le41} and \ref{le42} we have \[ \int J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))\dx a=\int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))\dx a \] for all $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $\varv$ with $W_\varv(1)=1$; the two lemmas give equal torus integrals.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.2 after translating by $n\in N$
nodes.statement: We replace $\varv$ by $\pi(n)\varv$ for any $n\in N$ and apply Lemma \ref{le21}, it follows that \[ J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))=\widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a)) \] for all $a\in \BCx$.
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $\varv$ by $\pi(n)\varv$ and invoking Lemma 2.2 gives pointwise equality in $a$.

nodes.name: Specialize to $a=1$
nodes.statement: Letting $a = 1$, the conclusion follows immediately.
nodes.statement_short: Set $a=1$ to conclude.

nodes.name: Proposition 5.4 (regularity of $J_{\sigma, \psi}$ on $S$)
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma $ and $\pi$ be as above. For any $h\in C_c^\infty(S)$, we have \[ J_{\sigma,\shskip \psi}(h)=\int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(s) ds. \] As such, we shall write $j_{\sigma, \shskip \psi} $ the restriction of $j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}$ on $S$.
nodes.statement_short: The Bessel distribution of $\sigma$ on $\SL_2(\BC)$ is represented by the restriction of $j_{\pi,\psi}$.
conclusions: J_{\sigma,\shskip \psi}(h)=\int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(s) ds.
As such, we shall write $j_{\sigma, \shskip \psi} $ the restriction of $j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}$ on $S$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.4
nodes.statement: Fix $h\in C_c^\infty(S)$. Let $U \subset Z$ be a small open neighborhood of the identity $1$ so that the map $ (s, z) \ra s z $ is an injection from $S \times U$ into $G = S \cdot Z$. Choose a function $\tw \in C_c^{\infty} (U)$ with \begin{align*} \int_{U} \tw(z) d z = 1, \end{align*} where $d z = \dx c$ if $z = z(c)$. Set $f (s z) = h (s) \omega_{\pi}\- (z) \tw (z) $. Clearly, $f$ is well defined and $f \in C_c^{\infty} (G)$ (indeed, $f \in C_c^{\infty} (S \cdot U)$). By Corollary \ref{cor53}, along with the $(\omega_{\pi}, Z)$-equivariance of $j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ (see \eqref{4eq: psi variant}), we have \begin{align*} J_{\pi,\shskip \psi}( f)&=\int_G f(g) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(g) dg = \int_{U} \tw(z)d z \int_Sh(s) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(s)ds = \int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(s)ds. \end{align*} On the other hand, since $\sigma$ is the restriction of $\pi$ to $S$, we may prove in a similar fashion that $\pi (f) \varv = \sigma (h) \varv$ for any $\varv \in H$. Precisely, \begin{align*} \int_G f(g)\pi(g)\varv \, dg = \int_{U } \tw(z)d z \int_S h(s) \pi(s)\varv \, ds = \int_S h(s) \sigma (s)\varv \, ds. \end{align*} In view of the definitions in \S \ref{sec: distributions}, it follows that $\varv_{L, \shskip f}=\varv_{L,\shskip h}$ and that $J_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(f)=J_{\sigma,\shskip \psi}(h)$. The proof is now completed.
nodes.statement_short: Spread $h$ over the centre by a bump function $\tw$, apply Corollary 5.3 and $(\omega_\pi,Z)$-equivariance, then match $\pi(f)=\sigma(h)$.

nodes.name: Construct $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$ from $h$
nodes.statement: Fix $h\in C_c^\infty(S)$. Let $U \subset Z$ be a small open neighborhood of the identity $1$ so that the map $ (s, z) \ra s z $ is an injection from $S \times U$ into $G = S \cdot Z$. Choose a function $\tw \in C_c^{\infty} (U)$ with \begin{align*} \int_{U} \tw(z) d z = 1, \end{align*} where $d z = \dx c$ if $z = z(c)$. Set $f (s z) = h (s) \omega_{\pi}\- (z) \tw (z) $. Clearly, $f$ is well defined and $f \in C_c^{\infty} (G)$ (indeed, $f \in C_c^{\infty} (S \cdot U)$).
nodes.statement_short: Choose a bump $\tw$ on a small central neighbourhood $U$ and set $f(sz)=h(s)\omega_\pi^{-1}(z)\tw(z)$.

nodes.name: Evaluate $J_{\pi,\psi}(f)$ by Corollary 5.3
nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{cor53}, along with the $(\omega_{\pi}, Z)$-equivariance of $j_{\pi, \shskip \psi}$ (see \eqref{4eq: psi variant}), we have \begin{align*} J_{\pi,\shskip \psi}( f)&=\int_G f(g) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(g) dg = \int_{U} \tw(z)d z \int_Sh(s) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(s)ds = \int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(s)ds. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 5.3 and central equivariance give $J_{\pi,\psi}(f)=\int_S h(s)j_{\pi,\psi}(s)ds$.

nodes.name: Show $\pi(f)\varv = \sigma(h)\varv$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since $\sigma$ is the restriction of $\pi$ to $S$, we may prove in a similar fashion that $\pi (f) \varv = \sigma (h) \varv$ for any $\varv \in H$. Precisely, \begin{align*} \int_G f(g)\pi(g)\varv \, dg = \int_{U } \tw(z)d z \int_S h(s) \pi(s)\varv \, ds = \int_S h(s) \sigma (s)\varv \, ds. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The same factorization shows the operators $\pi(f)$ and $\sigma(h)$ agree.

nodes.name: Identify the two Bessel distributions
nodes.statement: In view of the definitions in \S \ref{sec: distributions}, it follows that $\varv_{L, \shskip f}=\varv_{L,\shskip h}$ and that $J_{\pi,\shskip \psi}(f)=J_{\sigma,\shskip \psi}(h)$. The proof is now completed.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\varv_{L,f}=\varv_{L,h}$ and $J_{\pi,\psi}(f)=J_{\sigma,\psi}(h)$.

nodes.name: The $(N,N)$ orbital integral $O^{N,N}_{h, \psi}$
nodes.statement: For $h \in C_c^{\infty} (S)$ we introduced the orbital integral \begin{align} O^{N, \shskip N}_{h, \shskip \psi} (g) = \iint h (n(x) g n(y) ) \psi (x) \psi (y) d x d y. \end{align}

nodes.name: Absolute convergence of the $(N,N)$ orbital integral
nodes.statement: This orbital integral was studied by Jacquet. In particular, it is proven in \cite{Jacquet-RTF} that the integral in \eqref{eq: O NN (g)} converges absolutely for all $g \in X \cap S = N (A\cap S) \varw N$.
nodes.statement_short: Jacquet's $(N,N)$ orbital integral converges absolutely on the open Bruhat cell of $S$.
nodes.origin_citation: Jacquet, On the nonvanishing of some $L$-functions
assumptions: for all $g \in X \cap S = N (A\cap S) \varw N$.
conclusions: the integral in \eqref{eq: O NN (g)} converges absolutely

nodes.name: $J_{\sigma, \psi}$ as an integral of the $(N,N)$ orbital integral against $j_{\sigma, \psi}$
nodes.statement: In view of Proposition \ref{prop54: regularity of J on S}, along with \eqref{4eq: psi variant, SL}, for $h \in C_c^{\infty} (S)$ we have \begin{align} J_{\sigma,\shskip \psi} (h) = \int O^{N, \shskip N}_{h, \shskip \psi} (s(a) \varw) j_{\sigma,\shskip \psi} (s(a) \varw) \|a\|^{-2} \dx a. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Spectral side of the relative trace formula on $S$: $J_{\sigma,\psi}(h)=\int O^{N,N}_{h,\psi}(s(a)\varw)j_{\sigma,\psi}(s(a)\varw)\|a\|^{-2}\dx a$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform of a Schwartz function on $\BC$
nodes.statement: The Fourier transform $\widehat f $ of a Schwartz function $f$ on $\BC$ is defined by \begin{equation*} \widehat f (u) = \sideset{ }{_\BC }{\iint} \shskip f (z) e(- \Tr (uz) ) \shskip i d z \nwedge d \overline z. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Distributional Fourier transform formula for $\bfJ_{\mu, m}$
nodes.statement: According to \cite[Corollary 1.5]{Qi-II-G}, when $|\Re \mu | < \frac 1 2$ and $m$ is even, we have \begin{equation} \begin{split} \sideset{ }{_{\BC } }{\iint} \hskip - 2 pt \bfJ_{\mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp \widehat f (z) \frac {i d z \nwedge d \overline z} { {|z|}} = \frac 1 2 \sideset{ }{_{\BC } }{\iint} e \lp \Tr \lp \frac 1 {2 u} \rp \rp \hskip - 2 pt \bfJ_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\shskip \frac 1 2 m} \lp \frac 1 { 16 u ^{ 2} } \rp \hskip - 1 pt f (u) \frac {i d u \nwedge d \overline u} { {|u|}}, \end{split} \end{equation} if $f$ is a Schwartz function on $\BC$.
nodes.statement_short: Pairing $\bfJ_{\mu,m}$ with $\widehat f$ equals a pairing of $e(\Tr(1/2u))\bfJ_{\frac12\mu,\frac12 m}(1/16u^2)$ with $f$.
assumptions: if $f$ is a Schwartz function on $\BC$.
conclusions: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \sideset{ }{_{\BC } }{\iint} \hskip - 2 pt \bfJ_{\mu,\shskip m} \lp z \rp \widehat f (z) \frac {i d z \nwedge d \overline z} { {|z|}} = \frac 1 2 \sideset{ }{_{\BC } }{\iint} e \lp \Tr \lp \frac 1 {2 u} \rp \rp \hskip - 2 pt \bfJ_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\shskip \frac 1 2 m} \lp \frac 1 { 16 u ^{ 2} } \rp \hskip - 1 pt f (u) \frac {i d u \nwedge d \overline u} { {|u|}}, \end{split} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Remark on the test-function hypothesis in the Fourier formula
nodes.statement: It is critical that the test function $f$ in \eqref{6eq: Fourier transform of j} only need to be Schwartz on $\BC$ and rapid decay or vanishing at $0$ is not required. We also remark that the deduction from \eqref{eq: main 1} to \eqref{6eq: Fourier} is not so straightforward; see \cite[\S 6]{Qi-II-G} for more details.
nodes.statement_short: Only Schwartz decay is needed - no vanishing at $0$ - and the deduction from the integral formula is delicate.

nodes.name: Fourier formula rephrased for the Bessel function $j_{\pi, \psi}$
nodes.statement: Recall from \eqref{def: Fourier} that the Fourier transform with respect to the additive character $\psi (z) = \psi_{\lambdaup} (z) = e(\Tr(\lambdaup z))$ is defined by \begin{align*} \widehat f (u) = \int_{ \BC} f (z) \psi (uz) d z. \end{align*} Thus, in view of \eqref{4eq : j = J}, the identity \eqref{6eq: Fourier} may be rephrased as \begin{align} \sideset{ }{_{\BCx} }{\int} j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ) \widehat f (a) \dx a = \sideset{ }{_{\BCx} }{\int} e \lp \Tr ({\lambdaup} / {2 x} ) \rp \left| \lambdaup / 2 x \right| \bfJ_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\shskip \frac 1 2 m} \lp \lambdaup^2 / 16 x^2 \rp f (x ) { d x } , \end{align} if $f$ is a Schwartz function on $\BC$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrites the Qi formula as an identity pairing $j_{\pi,\psi}(t(a)\varw_0)$ with $\widehat f$ against an explicit $\bfJ_{\frac12\mu,\frac12 m}$ kernel.

nodes.name: $I(f)$ as a double integral against $j$ on $X$
nodes.statement: Let $X = A N \varw_0 N$. For $f \in C_c^{\infty} (X)$, since $ J $ is represented by the Bessel function $j = j_{\pi, \shskip \psi} $ on $X$ (Corollary \ref{cor53}), it follows that \begin{align} I (f) = \frac 1 {L (\pi, 1/2)} \int_{\BCx} \lp \int_{X} f(t(b)g) j (g) dg \rp \dx b . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: On the open cell, $I(f)$ is the torus average of $\int_X f(t(b)g)j(g)dg$ divided by $L(\pi,1/2)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 6.1 (relative Bessel distribution for split test functions)
nodes.statement: Let $f \in C_c^{\infty} (X)$ be of the form \begin{align} f (t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)) = f_1 (a) f_2 (c) f_3 (x) f_4 (y), \end{align} with $f_1, f_2 \in C_c^{\infty} (\BCx)$ and $f_3, f_4 \in C_c^{\infty} (\BC)$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \int_{\BCx} \int_{G} f(t(b)g) j (g) dg \shskip \dx b \\ = \ & \int_{\BCx} f_1 (b) \dx b \int_{\BCx} f_2 (c) \dx c \int_{\BC} f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int_{\BCx} j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a, \end{split} \end{equation} where $ \widehat f_2 $ is the $\psi$-Fourier transform of $f_2$ defined as in \eqref{def: Fourier}.
nodes.statement_short: For a product test function the double integral factors into four one-variable integrals, the last pairing $j(t(a)\varw_0)$ with $\widehat f_3$.
assumptions: Let $f \in C_c^{\infty} (X)$ be of the form \begin{align} f (t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)) = f_1 (a) f_2 (c) f_3 (x) f_4 (y), \end{align} with $f_1, f_2 \in C_c^{\infty} (\BCx)$ and $f_3, f_4 \in C_c^{\infty} (\BC)$.
conclusions: \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \int_{\BCx} \int_{G} f(t(b)g) j (g) dg \shskip \dx b \\ = \ & \int_{\BCx} f_1 (b) \dx b \int_{\BCx} f_2 (c) \dx c \int_{\BC} f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int_{\BCx} j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a, \end{split} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Let $dg = \dx a \hskip 1 pt \dx c \hskip 1 pt d x \hskip 1 pt d y$ be a Haar measure on $X$ for $g = t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)$. In view of \eqref{4eq: psi variant} and \eqref{6eq: f splits}, the integral on the left hand side of \eqref{6eq: double int for I} splits into the product \begin{align*} & \int f_2 (c) \dx c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int \lp \int f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \int f_3 (x) \psi ( a x) d x \shskip \dx a \rp \dx b \\ = \ & \int f_2 (c) \dx c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a \shskip \dx b. \end{align*} We claim that the last double integral converges absolutely. Hence we may change the order of integrations and the variable $b$ to $b/a$, getting \begin{align*} \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a \shskip \dx b & = \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \int f_1 (ab) \dx b \shskip \dx a \\ & = \int f_1 (b ) \dx b \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a. \end{align*} We now show the absolute convergence. Choose $|\Re \mu | < \rho < \frac 1 2$. Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} implies that $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ may be bounded by $|a|^{1 - 2\rho} + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. We can find positive constants $A$ and $B$ such that $f_1 (a ) \lll \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$, with $ \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$ defined to be the characteristic function on the annulus $\left\{ a : A \leqslant |a| \leqslant B \right\}$. Hence \begin{align*} \int \big| f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3(a) \big| \dx a \lll \int \Upsilon_{A/|b|, B/|b|} (a) \big|\widehat f_3 (a) \big| \big( |a|^{- 1- 2 \rho} + |a|^{- \frac 3 2} \big) d a. \end{align*} Since $\widehat f_3 (a)$ is rapidly decreasing when $|a|$ is large, it follows that the value of the integral above is rapidly decreasing when $|b|$ is small. When $|b|$ is large the integral is bounded by $ |b|^{2 \rho - 1} + |b|^{- \frac 1 2}$. It is then clear that integrating further with $\dx b = d b / |b|^2$ will converge absolutely at both $0$ and $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the Haar measure using $(\psi,N)$-equivariance, exchange integrations after checking absolute convergence with Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: Split the integral over the Bruhat cell
nodes.statement: Let $dg = \dx a \hskip 1 pt \dx c \hskip 1 pt d x \hskip 1 pt d y$ be a Haar measure on $X$ for $g = t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)$. In view of \eqref{4eq: psi variant} and \eqref{6eq: f splits}, the integral on the left hand side of \eqref{6eq: double int for I} splits into the product \begin{align*} & \int f_2 (c) \dx c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int \lp \int f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \int f_3 (x) \psi ( a x) d x \shskip \dx a \rp \dx b \\ = \ & \int f_2 (c) \dx c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a \shskip \dx b. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Equivariance and the product form split the integral into a product of one-variable integrals.

nodes.name: Exchange integrations and substitute $b \mapsto b/a$
nodes.statement: We claim that the last double integral converges absolutely. Hence we may change the order of integrations and the variable $b$ to $b/a$, getting \begin{align*} \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a \shskip \dx b & = \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \int f_1 (ab) \dx b \shskip \dx a \\ & = \int f_1 (b ) \dx b \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \dx a. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Assuming absolute convergence, swap the order and change variable to decouple $b$ from $a$.

nodes.name: Estimate using Lemma 4.1 and the support of $f_1$
nodes.statement: We now show the absolute convergence. Choose $|\Re \mu | < \rho < \frac 1 2$. Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} implies that $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ may be bounded by $|a|^{1 - 2\rho} + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. We can find positive constants $A$ and $B$ such that $f_1 (a ) \lll \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$, with $ \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$ defined to be the characteristic function on the annulus $\left\{ a : A \leqslant |a| \leqslant B \right\}$. Hence \begin{align*} \int \big| f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3(a) \big| \dx a \lll \int \Upsilon_{A/|b|, B/|b|} (a) \big|\widehat f_3 (a) \big| \big( |a|^{- 1- 2 \rho} + |a|^{- \frac 3 2} \big) d a. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $j(t(a)\varw_0)$ by Lemma 4.1 and $f_1$ by an annulus indicator.

nodes.name: Conclude absolute convergence at $0$ and $\infty$
nodes.statement: Since $\widehat f_3 (a)$ is rapidly decreasing when $|a|$ is large, it follows that the value of the integral above is rapidly decreasing when $|b|$ is small. When $|b|$ is large the integral is bounded by $ |b|^{2 \rho - 1} + |b|^{- \frac 1 2}$. It is then clear that integrating further with $\dx b = d b / |b|^2$ will converge absolutely at both $0$ and $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Rapid decay of $\widehat f_3$ gives convergence of the $b$-integral at both ends.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.2
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be the distribution on $G$ defined by the difference $T=I-\widetilde I$. First, in view of \eqref{6eq: I = int of i}, $I$ and $\widetilde I$ coincide on $X$, so $T$ is supported on the Borel $B = G\smallsetminus X$. Second, it is clear that $T$ satisfies $\rho_r(n(y))I=\psi(y)I$. Third, we claim that $T$ is an eigen-distribution of the Casimir element $\varDelta$ in the universal enveloping algebra of the Lie algebra of $G$. To see this, we first note that $I$ is an eigen-distribution of $\varDelta$ according to \cite[\S 3]{Shalika-MO}, that is, $\varDelta I= \kappa I$ ($\kappa \in \BC$). As aforementioned, $I$ is represented by the (real analytic) function $i$ when restricted on $ U $, so $i$ is an eigen-function of $\varDelta$ on $U$. Precisely, we have $\varDelta \shskip i = \kappa \shskip i$, which further implies $\varDelta \widetilde I= \kappa \widetilde I$. The third claim is now proven. Under the three conditions above, by \cite[Proposition 2.10]{Shalika-MO}, we must have $T=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the difference $T=I-\widetilde I$ is supported on the Borel, is $(\psi,N)$-equivariant and a Casimir eigen-distribution, then apply Shalika's Proposition 2.10.

nodes.name: The character $\psi^D$ and the Weil factor $\gamma (z, \psi^D)$
nodes.statement: Fix the nontrivial additive character $ \psi = \psi_{\lambdaup}$ of $\BC$ defined by $\psi (z) = e (\Tr (\lambdaup z) )$. Let $D \in \BCx$ and define $ \psi^D (z) = \psi (D z)$. Define the Weil factor $\gamma (z, \psi^D) $ by \begin{align*} \gamma (z, \psi^D) = 1/{\textstyle \sqrt {\|2 D\|}} . \end{align*} Note that $ \gamma (z, \psi^D)$ does not depend on $z$, but we would rather keep $z$ in this conventional notation.
nodes.statement_short: Sets $\psi^D(z)=\psi(Dz)$ and $\gamma(z,\psi^D)=1/\sqrt{\|2D\|}$, independent of $z$.

nodes.name: The transfer factor $\Delta_{D, \psi}$
nodes.statement: Define a {transfer factor} \begin{align} \Delta_{D,\shskip \psi} (z) = \gamma (z, \psi^D) \psi (2D/ z) {\textstyle \sqrt {\|z\|} }. \end{align}

nodes.name: Remark on re-normalizing $j_{\sigma, \psi^D}$ when changing the character
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma$ be an irreducible unitary representation of $S$. When changing $\psi = \psi_{\lambdaup}$ to $\psi^D = \psi_{\lambdaup D}$, we wish to keep the Haar measure fixed on $S$ with respect to $\psi $ and instead re-normalize the formulae of $ j_{\sigma,\shskip \psi^D } $ in \S \ref{sec: Bessel, GL2} by an extra factor $ \sqrt {\|D\|} $\footnote{In the paper \cite{BaruchMao-Real}, the more reasonable re-normalizing factor should be $\sqrt {|D|}$ not $1/\sqrt {|D|}$, so their formulae (19.2) and (19.4) need small modifications on the factors involving $|D|$.}.
nodes.statement_short: Keep the Haar measure fixed and instead re-normalize $j_{\sigma,\psi^D}$ by $\sqrt{\|D\|}$.

nodes.name: Definition 8.1 (the Bessel identity: $\sigma$ corresponds to $\pi$)
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ be an irreducible unitary representation of $G / Z$. We say that an irreducible unitary representation $\sigma$ of $S$ corresponds to $\pi$ if the following equality {\rm(}Bessel identity{\rm)} holds \begin{align} i_{\pi, \shskip \psi} (n (z/ 4 D)\varw_0) = \frac {4 \Delta_{D,\shskip \psi} (z) \epsilon (\pi, 1/2, \psi) } {L(\pi, 1/2)} j_{\sigma, \shskip \psi^D} (\varw s (z)), \end{align} for all $z \in \BCx$.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma$ corresponds to $\pi$ when the relative Bessel function of $\pi$ equals $4\Delta_{D,\psi}\epsilon/L$ times the Bessel function of $\sigma$.

nodes.statement: For each irreducible unitary representation $\pi$ of $G / Z$, there exists a corresponding irreducible unitary representation $\sigma $ of $S$ satisfying the Bessel identity \eqref{eq: Bessel indentity}.
